doc.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Rhythm sections, Shorty's band, Nat Pierce and Diva
summary: Basie-fan rhythm section in Shorty Sherock's wartime band, how Nat Pierce joined, and the all-girl Diva band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: We’ll move back to the Basie band for just a minute. There’s been — people always talk about their rhythm section, and what made that so special. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-

You know that rhythm section really characterized different bands. If they played that style, that was their ideal. And when Shorty Sherock got his big band and got a date at Glen Island Casino, his rhythm section were Basie fans. As a matter of fact, Nat Pierce, you may have heard of him, he was a noted arranger and pianist, and before he died they formed a, what do they called it, Juggernaut band.
The Juggernaut band, in fact we talked to Frank Capp in Los Angeles.

Oh did you? Well Nat I think this was his first professional job. Stanley Kay, the drummer with Shorty Sherock’s orchestra was in a record store in Boston buying some Basie records. And before he got, they had little booths in those days. You went in a little glass-enclosed booth and there were individual machines, you could play records. So as he hadn’t even put his records on the turntable, and he heard the very ones that he was buying from the next booth. He thought, I’ve got to meet this guy. And he went in and he said, “you’ve got the same records I have.” And the man said, “oh I do?” Stanley said, “are you a musician by any chance?” He said, “what’s your instrument.” “Piano.” Stanley said, “are you free tonight? We need a piano player.” And so Nat came on the band. And so there was Stanley and I guess they brainwashed the bassist to be in their camp. But the brass section were Italian chaps, and they played a different way. And I thought it was like you were having a race war on the stage every night. They were out of sync. They weren’t moving like the rhythm section. It was funny. But that was Shorty’s band. Well it was wartime you know. You took what you could get. Although Brew Moore was in the sax section. He had an interesting band.
Do you still see the Basie band in their present form?

Yeah, I think they’re not — they’re getting away from it and, God knows the Ellington band, I mean they rarely, they’re way off someplace. They’re not in the — the old dyed- in-the-wool fans, they want to hear that stuff. I’ll tell you who plays like Basie is Diva, the all-girl band if you’ve heard them. Because Stanley Kay is the founding father of that band, and he manages them, and he writes little things that sound like Basie. He has a take off on Four Brothers. He calls it “Three Sisters and a Cousin.” Saxophones get up. The only thing about them, they’re wonderful and they sound like Basie, but they play too loud. And it’s because they’re females I guess. They want to show they can do it.
